title: Exploring soundscaping options for the cognitive environment in an open-plan office
research_question: This study aims to understand the relationship between various types of soundscapes and knowledge worker cognitive performance as well as perception.

participants.description: 16 participants (12 male, 4 female; 75%:25% gender ratio) from a large pharmaceutical company in the United Kingdom, aged from early 1920s to late 1950s, reported as fit and healthy for work.
participants.recruitment: Email invitation sent to employees of the company, recruited on a voluntary basis.

stimuli_or_exposures.description: Four acoustic conditions simulating an open-plan office: (1) no office noise, (2) typical daily office noise, (3) white noise plus typical daily office noise background, and (4) spring water sound plus typical daily office noise background. Office noise played at ~60 dBA, white noise and spring water at 44–45 dBA.

mechanisms: Psychological preference for silence for highly focused cognitive tasks.
Mental alertness modulation by certain levels of sound/noise.
Higher mental effort, attention, or arousal indicated by SCRs under specific sound conditions.
Overstimulation of cognition by higher arousal leading to poorer performance.
implementation_implications: Discrepancy between cognitive performance and subjective satisfaction/preference suggests that complete silence, while preferred, may not always lead to the best performance.
A certain level of sound/noise might help with mental alertness.

Careful attention to environmental details (geometry, sound absorption, speaker location, sound quality, job functions, other noises) is necessary to replicate positive effects of water masking sounds.
Implementing quiet spaces/zones in open-plan offices is critical for focus work modes, as silence was greatly preferred for intensive cognitive tasks.
Providing diverse acoustic environments and flexibility for individuals to move between them is important due to individual differences in noise perception and sensitivity.

limitations: Small sample size (N=16) and relatively homogeneous group (age range, gender ratio, shared office space team).

The experimental setup, while following professional recommendations, may not have accurately simulated the acoustic environment of a real open-plan office (e.g., close proximity between participants and sound system, specific acoustic properties).
The study did not cover all possible sound options.

Statistical analysis limitation in cognitive performance assessment due to a small sample size and a huge range of constant numbers in the independent variable, leading to no observed statistical significance despite descriptive differences.
The study did not investigate auditory and visual impacts of nature sound masking options by integrating visuals together.

paper_metadata.title: Exploring soundscaping options for the cognitive environment in an open-plan office
paper_metadata.crossref_title: Exploring soundscaping options for the cognitive environment in an open-plan office
paper_metadata.crossref_abstract: A major source of noise complaints in open-plan offices has consistently been co-workers talking nearby or talking on the phone. Various masking sounds such as white noise and pink noise have been explored to reduce the intelligibility level of speech from adjacent co-workers in open-plan offices. Recently, nature soundscapes such as water, rainfall or birdsong have been introduced instead of conventional white or pink noises. Water sounds with limited acoustic variation have shown more effectiveness than nature sounds with high acoustic variation such as birdsong. This study examined four types of background sounds in a controlled lab environment that simulated a typical open-plan office in a large pharmaceutical company in the United Kingdom. The purpose was to understand cognitive performance, satisfaction and preference, and physiological responses among the four types of background sounds: no external acoustic noise, typical daily office noise, white noise and spring water sound. The study employed three methods: an assessment of cognitive performance to measure memory, distractibility and decision-making; a survey to understand subjective satisfaction and preference; and use of wearable devices to monitor physiological responses. Two different types of wearable devices were used: pulse oximeter and electrodermal activity sensor to compare physiological responses to the four types of sounds. This article discusses discrepancies found between participants’ satisfaction/preference and their cognitive performance under the four background sounds and potential future implications of masking sounds in open-plan offices.

theory_commitments.specific_claim: Natural soundscapes can restore directed attention and improve cognitive performance in distracting environments.

mechanism_chain.description: Different soundscapes influence perceived distraction and cognitive load, which in turn affects concentration and satisfaction.

steps.from_construct: Acoustic condition (e.g., speech vs. nature sound)

instruments_used.name: Arithmetic task
instruments_used.description: Mental arithmetic calculations performed under time pressure

instruments_used.name: Self-report questionnaire
instruments_used.description: Likert-scale rating of participants' ability to concentrate in the given acoustic environment

instruments_used.name: NASA-TLX
instruments_used.description: Mental effort rating scale assessing six dimensions of workload

instruments_used.name: Perceived Restorativeness Scale (PRS)
instruments_used.description: Scale measuring feelings of being away, fascination, extent, and compatibility in an environment
